title: Usage
text:
Solving
using PlasticIceSheet

z_s, H = solve(z_b, τ_b, mask; dx, dy)







argument
meaning




z_b
bed elevation z_b (m), nx × ny matrix


τ_b
basal shear stress (Pa), scalar or field


mask
true where grounded ice exists; the margin is the mask boundary


dx, dy
grid spacings (m)



Returns (z_s, H), the surface elevation and thickness. Ice-free cells have H = 0 and z_s = z_b. Pad the mask with at least one ice-free cell, since an ice region without an ice-free cell is unreachable (it is returned with H = 0 and a warning).
Keyword options (see the solve docstring for the rest):

mode: :surface (default) solves the plastic surface equation directly over any bed relief, in one sweep solve. :flat solves the flat-bed eikonal for H^2 and drapes it on the bed; it is the cheapest mode and equals :surface on a flat bed. :full adds the bed gradient to the H^2 equation by a damped fixed point (n_outer, outer_tol, relax); it is kept for comparison and does not converge on rough real beds (Algorithms §3).
z_ss: sea level (m), scalar or field. Marine margins are grounded at the flotation thickness (\rho_w/\rho_i)\max(z_{ss} - z_b, 0).
margin: where the margin lies between an ice cell and its ice-free neighbour. :face (default) puts it on the cell face, :centre on the ice-free cell centre (the behaviour before v0.2), and a field margin_frac ∈ [0, 1) gives its distance from the ice-free cell centre as a fraction of the spacing (Algorithms §6).
params: a PlasticParams with the densities ρ_i, ρ_w, gravity g and the thickness floor H_min.

A margin known as a signed distance (m, positive in the ice) converts to margin_frac:
frac = margin_frac_from_sdist(sdist, mask, dx, dy)
z_s, H = solve(z_b, τ_b, mask; dx, dy, margin = frac)
On a 300 × 300 grid a :surface solve takes about 6 ms, :flat about 3 ms and a converging :full solve about 1 s.

Diagnostics
ice_volume(H, dx, dy)                          # m³
ice_area(mask, dx, dy)                         # m²
surface_misfit(z_s, z_s_obs, mask)             # mean-squared surface misfit over ice
r = stress_residual(z_s, z_b, τ_b, mask; dx, dy)   # |ρ_i g H |∇z_s| − τ_b| / τ_b per cell
stress_residual checks how well a geometry satisfies the plastic stress balance, in any mode. It is a cell-centred measure and is of order 1 at the first ice cell (the one-sided slope of a square-root profile), so read it away from the margin. On a 300 m bed bump the median over the interior is about 0.04 for :surface and 0.5 for :flat.

title: Usage
text:
Velocity and surface mass balance
The plastic solve returns only geometry. A DIVA closure on the fixed geometry recovers a depth-averaged velocity and a first-order SMB (Algorithms §8). Pick a rheology and a sliding law:
rheology = GlenRheology(A = 1.0e-16, n = 3.0)            # isothermal Glen, per year
sliding  = WeertmanSliding(β = 1.0e4, m = 3.0)           # or LinearSliding(β),
                                                         # RegularizedCoulomb(C, u_0, m; u_max)
The coefficient (β, or C for RegularizedCoulomb) may be a field of the grid’s shape. RegularizedCoulomb returns a NaN sliding speed where τ_b ≥ C, since the bed is at its Coulomb cap and the speed is undetermined. With a finite speed cap u_max, the speed is min(u_b, u_max) instead, and u_max at the cap.

Closure B: velocity, then implied SMB
vel = diva_velocity(z_s, H, τ_b, mask, dx, dy; rheology, sliding)
# named tuple: ux, uy, speed, u_b (sliding), u_def (deformation), ex, ey (flow direction)

smb = smb_from_velocity(vel, H, z_s, mask, dx, dy)      # ḃ = ∇·(ūH), MFD operator


Closure A: balance velocity from a prescribed SMB
bal = balance_velocity(z_s, H, mask, smb, dx, dy)       # named tuple: speed, ux, uy, Q, ...
ib  = implied_basal_velocity(z_s, H, τ_b, mask, smb, dx, dy; rheology)
# ib.u_basal = u_balance − u_def: the basal velocity that geometry and SMB demand
balance_flux is the exact inverse of smb_from_velocity, so routing closure B’s SMB back through closure A recovers closure B’s flux to machine precision.


SMB-driven reconstruction
The dual of solve drives the geometry with an SMB (m ice yr⁻¹) instead of a yield stress, on the same fixed margin (Algorithms §9):
z_s, H = diva_reconstruct(z_b, mask, smb, dx, dy; rheology, sliding, z_ss)
The default method = :steady solves steady mass conservation \nabla\cdot\mathbf q = \dot b with H \ge 0 directly. Mask cells where ablation exceeds the inflow end ice-free. It stops when the residual falls below res_tol (m yr⁻¹) and warns otherwise. On Greenland at 16 km (examples/reconstruct_greenland.jl) it takes a few seconds.
The implied SMB of this method for a given geometry, with the margin outflow and the surface velocity of the same closure, is:
o = smb_flux_divergence(z_b, H, mask, dx, dy; rheology, sliding, z_ss, τ_cap = τ_b)
# named tuple: smb, q_land, q_marine (outflow per margin cell), us_x, us_y
The geometry H is a root of the steady problem forced by o.smb. τ_cap (optional) caps the driving stress of the fluxes, since a plastic bed carries at most its yield stress.
method = :routing keeps the earlier iteration (route the SMB, invert the flux law for the driving stress, plastic sweep, under-relax). It is stable only for relax below roughly slope × Δx / H, i.e., 0.003–0.04 in tests, and is kept for comparison.

title: Usage
text:
Inverting for \tau_b
The solver is differentiable with respect to \tau_b (Algorithms §7).

Forward mode: scalar or low-dimensional \tau_b
using ForwardDiff
loss(τ_b) = surface_misfit(first(solve(z_b, τ_b, mask; dx, dy)), z_s_obs, mask)
g = ForwardDiff.derivative(loss, 1.0e5)


Reverse mode: a full per-cell \tau_b field
Load the extension triggers, then differentiate differentiable_thickness with any reverse-mode AD:
using ImplicitDifferentiation, ADTypes, ForwardDiff, Zygote

loss(τ_b) = surface_misfit(differentiable_thickness(τ_b, z_b, mask; dx, dy) .+ z_b, z_s_obs, mask)
g = Zygote.gradient(loss, τ_b)[1]      # gradient with respect to the whole τ_b field
differentiable_thickness takes the same mode, z_ss and margin keywords as solve. The default reverse-mode linear solver is direct, which is robust for modest grids. For very large fields, pass an iterative solver (see the differentiable_thickness docstring).
examples/invert_tau.jl recovers a spatially varying \tau_b from an observed surface with Adam, and Inversion covers the parameterizations of \tau_b on real data.

title: Usage
text:
NetCDF I/O
using NCDatasets

inp = load_plastic_inputs("inputs.nc")             # (; z_b, τ_b, mask, dx, dy, x, y)
z_s, H = solve(inp.z_b, inp.τ_b, inp.mask; inp.dx, inp.dy)
save_reconstruction("out.nc", z_s, H; x = inp.x, y = inp.y)

title: Usage
text:
Caveats

The geometry is steady state only. It is biased thick where the real ice was streaming or otherwise dynamic, since the plastic assumption sees no reduced driving stress there.
\tau_b carries essentially all of the uncertainty. For a first guess a constant (about 50–100 kPa) or a bed-keyed value is reasonable, but the result is not a constrained reconstruction.
:surface and :flat are first-order accurate. At 10–30 km the margin position and the coarse inputs change the ice volume by several percent (Algorithms §6).

title: Usage
text:
Fortran library
PlasticIceSheet is a dependency-free Fortran port of the forward solver and the closures (libplastic.a), for coupling into Fortran models. It uses the same schemes (results were verified bit-identical against v0.1) and adds a warm start, OpenMP parallelism and a joint inversion of speed and SMB. The \tau_b inversion and the AD extension remain Julia-only.

title: Algorithms
text: This page describes how PlasticIceSheet.jl turns a margin, a bed and a basal shear stress into an ice sheet, how it differentiates the result with respect to the shear stress, and how the same discretization supports velocity, surface-mass-balance and SMB-driven reconstructions.

title: Algorithms
text:
1. The governing equation
The reconstruction assumes perfectly plastic, steady-state ice. In that limit the basal shear stress balances the gravitational driving stress,

\tau_b = \tau_d = \rho_i\, g\, H\, |\nabla z_s| ,
\tag{1}
where the driving stress is set by the ice geometry. In a reconstruction \tau_b is prescribed (it is the field we choose or invert for) and the surface is the unknown. Rearranging for the surface slope gives the equation we solve:

|\nabla z_s| = \frac{k}{H} = \frac{k}{z_s - z_b}, \qquad k = \frac{\tau_b}{\rho_i\, g} .
\tag{2}
Equation 2 is a static Hamilton–Jacobi equation. The surface is built inward from the margin, where H \to 0, and its upwind (viscosity) solution yields the correct envelope wherever ice from different margins meets. Ice divides, domes and merging ice caps therefore appear without any flowline or saddle handling. This is the physics of ICESHEET 2.0 (Gowan et al., 2016), solved on a grid rather than by tracing characteristics.
Three solver modes discretize Equation 2. :surface (the default) solves it for z_s directly (§2). :flat and :full solve it for w = H^2 (§3). The former is exact on a flat bed and the latter adds the bed gradient through an outer fixed point.

title: Algorithms
text:
2. :surface mode
:surface solves Equation 2 for u = z_s in one fast-sweeping solve, with no outer iteration. Its Hamiltonian, |p| - k/(u - z_b), increases with u, since the right-hand side depends on z_s only through the thickness of the cell itself. The equation is therefore proper, and a monotone upwind scheme converges to its viscosity solution by fast sweeping (§5).
The discretization integrates the margin singularity. A cell-centred form, (u-a)_+^2/\Delta x^2 + \ldots = (k/(u - z_b))^2, is also monotone but inaccurate at the margin: on a flat bed its first ice cell is \sqrt{k\,\Delta x} thick instead of the Nye value \sqrt{2k\,\Delta x} (about 29 % low at every resolution). We therefore take each axis difference times the edge-mean thickness, with the neighbour thickness measured from the bed of the cell:

P_a(H) = \frac{(H - \alpha)_+ \,(H + \alpha_+)}{2}, \quad \alpha = a - z_b, \qquad
\left(\frac{P_a(H)}{\Delta x}\right)^{2} + \left(\frac{P_b(H)}{\Delta y}\right)^{2} = k^2 ,
\tag{3}
where a and b are the upwind (smaller) neighbour surfaces along x and y, and \alpha_+ = \max(\alpha, 0). P_a increases with H and does not increase with a, so the scheme is proper and monotone. Where both neighbour surfaces stand above the bed of the cell, Equation 3 is the w-eikonal of §3 with w_a = \alpha^2 and has a closed-form root. Otherwise the root is found by Newton iteration from the smaller one-sided root, which decreases monotonically to the solution since P^2 is convex there. This is godunov_surface.
On a flat bed :surface is identical to :flat, including the exact 1-D Nye profile. Over bed relief it converges at first order: for a 1-D bed with slope 5\times10^{-3}, the maximum error against an ODE reference halves with each halving of \Delta x (about 1 m at \Delta x = 500 m), while :flat is off by about 300 m. On real beds at 32 km (GRL-32KM and NH-32KM) it converges in about 10 sweeps, while the :full fixed point does not converge for any relaxation tested (§3). These real-data results come from the Fortran port of the package, which uses the same scheme. For these reasons :surface is the default.

title: Algorithms

On a flat bed, multiplying Equation 2 by 2H and using 
abla(H^2) = 2H

with a finite right-hand side and the regular margin condition w = H_{flt}^2. :flat solves Equation 4 and drapes the thickness on the bed (z_s = z_b + \sqrt{w}). It is the cheapest mode and exact when bed relief is small compared with the ice thickness. Over relief, however, the surface follows the bed, which biases the thickness by a few hundred metres at 32 km on Greenland.
:full adds the bed gradient. Writing 
abla z_s = 
abla H +

|

On GRL-32KM and NH-32KM, in contrast, it oscillates globally for every relaxation tested (0.4 to 0.02, 2000 iterations). :full is therefore kept for comparison with earlier results only.

title: Algorithms
text:
4. The Godunov update
The eikonal |\nabla u| = F of :flat and :full is discretized cell by cell with the first-order Godunov upwind scheme. With a and b the smaller neighbour values along each axis,

a = \min(u_{i-1,j},\, u_{i+1,j}), \qquad b = \min(u_{i,j-1},\, u_{i,j+1}),

the update is the smallest u satisfying

\left(\frac{(u-a)_+}{\Delta x}\right)^{2} + \left(\frac{(u-b)_+}{\Delta y}\right)^{2} = F^2 .

The two-sided root is accepted if it exceeds both neighbours, and otherwise the smaller one-sided update \min(a + F\,\Delta x,\; b + F\,\Delta y) applies. This is godunov_eikonal. Both kernels are pure functions without mutation or indexing, which lets the AD back ends differentiate them directly.
Where an ice-free neighbour lies closer than a full spacing (a sub-cell margin, §6), the two sides of an axis have different spacings. The upwind term of that axis is then the maximum over the sides of (u - a_s)_+/d_s, and the update is the minimum over the side combinations. Each candidate is monotone, so the minimum is too.

title: Algorithms
text:
5. Fast sweeping
The discrete equations are solved by the fast-sweeping method: Gauss–Seidel updates that keep the monotone minimum, u_{i,j} \leftarrow \min(u_{i,j},\ \text{update}), over the four diagonal traversal orderings in rotation. Each ordering follows the characteristics of one quadrant of directions, so a few sweeps converge the whole field in O(N) work. Ice cells start at +\infty and ice-free cells hold their boundary value (§6). An ice region with no ice-free cell is never reached; its cells are returned with H = 0 and a warning.

title: Algorithms
text:
6. Boundary conditions and margin position
Ice-free cells carry the Dirichlet value of the margin. On land (z_b \ge z_{ss}) the margin thickness is zero. At a marine margin (z_b < z_{ss}) the grounding line sits at the flotation thickness,

H_{flt} = \frac{\rho_w}{\rho_i}\,\max(z_{ss} - z_b,\, 0),

which reproduces the marine treatment of ICESHEET. Sea level z_ss is an input like the bed and may be a field. The margin value is z_b + H_{flt} in :surface and H_{flt}^2 in :flat and :full.
The margin lies between an ice cell and its ice-free neighbour. The margin keyword sets where: the ice-free neighbour enters the update at (1 - f)\,\Delta x from the ice-cell centre, with f = 1/2 for :face (the default; margin on the cell face), f = 0 for :centre (margin on the ice-free cell centre, the behaviour before v0.2), or a field f \in [0, 1) on the ice-free cells. A margin closer than 1 % of a spacing to an ice-cell centre counts as at 1 %, which keeps the update well conditioned. For a margin given as a signed distance (positive in the ice), margin_frac_from_sdist returns f = -s_{dist}/\sqrt{\Delta x\,\Delta y} on the ice-free cells next to the ice. This value is isotropic and thus exact for margins along a grid axis.
The margin position matters at coarse resolution. For a circular cap of radius 30 km on a flat bed (centre off the grid), the volume error relative to the exact solution is:

title: Algorithms
text:
7. Differentiating with respect to \tau_b
The solver is a pure function of \tau_b, so any objective on the output (a misfit to an observed surface, a target volume) is differentiable. This enables basal-shear-stress inversion (Inversion).
For a scalar \tau_b or a low-dimensional parameterization, ForwardDiff differentiates through solve. The cost scales with the number of parameters.
For a full per-cell field, the converged working field u (z_s or w) instead satisfies the Godunov residual

r_{i,j}(u, \tau_b) = u_{i,j} - \bigl(\text{Godunov update at } (i,j)\bigr) = 0

on ice cells (and u - \text{bc} = 0 elsewhere). By the implicit function theorem, for a loss L(u),

\frac{\partial L}{\partial \tau_b}
= -\,\frac{\partial L}{\partial u}\left(\frac{\partial r}{\partial u}\right)^{-1}\frac{\partial r}{\partial \tau_b},

so the gradient costs one linear solve with the residual Jacobian, independent of the number of sweeps or outer iterations. Only the residual is differentiated (with ForwardDiff). This is wired up with ImplicitDifferentiation.jl in a package extension, so any reverse-mode AD (e.g., Zygote) obtains the gradient through differentiable_thickness. The :surface and :flat gradients agree with forward mode to machine precision. The :full gradient is exact only where the damped forward solve has driven the residual to zero.






NoteNaN hygiene



\sqrt{w} has an infinite derivative at w = 0. Wherever it is differentiated it is floored at H_{\min}^2, since the unguarded derivative produces \infty\cdot 0 = \text{NaN} in the reverse pass. :surface avoids the square root altogether.

title: Algorithms
text:
8. Velocity and surface mass balance
The plastic solve returns geometry and nothing else. The perfectly plastic (n\to\infty) limit discards the rate-dependent information that a rate factor, a velocity and a surface mass balance (SMB) carry, so recovering them requires one extra closure on the fixed geometry.
The plastic balance Equation 1 is the membrane-free limit of the SSA/DIVA momentum balance: with \tau_d = \tau_b and the basal drag opposing flow, the divergence of the longitudinal stresses vanishes. The velocity is therefore local and analytical, and the ice flows down the surface gradient, \hat{\mathbf u} = -\nabla z_s/|\nabla z_s|. The geometry fixes the flow direction but not the flux magnitude. Closing that gap needs one assumption, which can be made in two dual ways.

Closure B: parameters → velocity → SMB
Assume a rheology and a sliding law. The depth-averaged speed is the sum of basal sliding and internal deformation, both at the local driving stress \tau = \tau_b:

|\bar{\mathbf u}| = u_b(\tau_b) + \frac{2A}{n+2}\,\tau_b^{\,n}\,H .
\tag{6}
The deformational term is the SIA closed form with \tau_d = \tau_b, and u_b inverts the sliding law (basal_velocity). The sliding coefficient (\beta or C) may be a field. For a regularized-Coulomb bed at its cap the sliding speed is undetermined and is returned as NaN, unless a speed cap u_max is given. Steady-state mass conservation then gives the implied SMB as the flux divergence, \dot b = \nabla\cdot(\bar{\mathbf u}\,H) (diva_velocity, smb_from_velocity). The velocity is a smooth function of \tau_b, so the closure doubles as an observation operator for inversion.


Closure A: SMB → velocity
The dual prescribes \dot b and routes it down the fixed surface for the flux the ice must carry in steady state, the balance velocity (Budd and Warner, 1996): \nabla\cdot\mathbf q = \dot b, \mathbf q \parallel \hat{\mathbf u}, |\bar{\mathbf u}| = |\mathbf q|/H (balance_flux, balance_velocity).
Both closures use one finite-volume multiple-flow-direction (MFD) operator, which partitions the throughput of a cell to its lower ice neighbours in proportion to their surface drop. Routing and the implied-SMB divergence use the same weights, so balance_flux(smb_from_velocity(u)) returns \bar{\mathbf u} H to machine precision. Subtracting the deformation Equation 6 from the balance speed leaves the basal velocity that geometry and SMB jointly demand (implied_basal_velocity). This is a check on whether the plastic geometry and an assumed climate are consistent with a plausible bed.

title: Algorithms
text:
9. SMB-driven reconstruction
The closures also support the dual of solve: reconstruct the geometry driven by an SMB instead of a yield stress, on the same prescribed margin (diva_reconstruct). Two methods are available. :steady (the default) solves steady mass conservation directly. :routing derives \tau_b by routing and is only conditionally stable.

:steady: steady mass conservation
The unknown is H \ge 0 on the ice cells, with the membrane-free DIVA flux of Equation 6 and the driving stress taken from the geometry:

\mathbf q = -H\,U(\tau, H)\,\frac{\nabla z_s}{|\nabla z_s|}, \qquad
\tau = \rho_i g H |\nabla z_s|, \qquad U = u_b(\tau) + \frac{2A}{n+2}\tau^n H .

With the obstacle H \ge 0, steady state is the complementarity problem

H \ge 0, \qquad F(H) = \nabla\cdot\mathbf q - \dot b \ge 0, \qquad H\,F(H) = 0 ,

where F > 0 at H = 0 marks a cell where ablation exceeds the inflow. This is the steady SIA with sliding, a monotone degenerate-elliptic problem with a unique solution.
Fluxes are staggered on the cell faces. Between two ice cells the face thickness is the mean where the surface drop \Delta s across the face is small against the upstream thickness, and limited towards the upstream value where it is not (downstream weight \min(1/2,\ H_{up}/(4\Delta s))). This keeps the face flux non-increasing in the downstream thickness, so F is non-increasing in the neighbouring thicknesses, as the active-set Newton step requires. The tangential slope is the mean of the central differences at the two cells. Between an ice cell and an ice-free neighbour the flux is the one-sided SIA flux to the margin, which lies at the margin position of §6. It uses the slope and the mean thickness of the segment between cell centre and margin, and never flows inward. Unlike the plastic profile, whose flux tends to zero at a land margin, this flux grows with the thickness of the ice cell, so every SMB has a steady state. For a Coulomb bed without a speed cap, the driving stress of the fluxes is capped at 0.999\,C.
The implied SMB of a geometry is the divergence of the same face fluxes (smb_flux_divergence). A geometry forced by its own implied SMB is therefore a root of F. smb_flux_divergence also returns the outflow through the margin faces of each ice cell, split into land and marine (an ice-free neighbour below sea level), and the surface velocity of the same closure. An optional τ_cap limits the driving stress of the fluxes, e.g., to \tau_b, since a plastic bed carries at most its yield stress.
The solver is pseudo-transient continuation with one semismooth Newton step per pseudo-time step. Each step solves \Phi(H) = \min\!\bigl(H,\ c\,G(H)\bigr) = 0 for G(H) = (H - H_k)/\Delta t + F(H), where a cell is active (H = 0) when its own Newton step would empty it. The Jacobian \partial F/\partial H is computed by finite differences with nine colours, since F at a cell depends only on the 3\times3 block around it. The linear system over the inactive cells is solved directly (SparseArrays). The new iterate is \max(H + \lambda\,\delta H, 0), with \lambda halved until the rms residual decreases. The pseudo-time step grows by switched evolution relaxation (at least 1.5× after a step that does not increase the residual), and the iteration stops when \max|\min(H, F)| falls below res_tol. The pseudo-time term keeps the system well posed at divides, where \partial F/\partial H vanishes with the surface slope.
In tests the method recovers the plastic geometry from a cold start under its own implied SMB to about 10^{-12} m in a few tens of steps. For the Vialov profile (n = 3, \dot b = 0.3 m yr⁻¹, L = 300 km) the maximum relative error is about 2.6, 1.1, 0.6 and 0.3 % at \Delta x = 20, 10, 5 and 2.5 km, i.e., first order.


:routing: derived yield stress
:routing iterates the plastic solve with \tau_b derived from the SMB: (1) route \dot b down the current surface for the throughput (§8), (2) invert the flux law Equation 6 per cell for the driving stress that carries it (bisection), (3) solve the plastic equation with that stress (inner_mode), and (4) under-relax and repeat. A plastic solution forced by its own closure-B SMB is an exact fixed point of this map.
The map is, however, only conditionally stable. The MFD weights split the flux of a cell by surface drops of slope × \Delta x, i.e., a few metres, so a thickness change \delta H moves the split, the throughput and the derived stress by O(\delta H/(\text{slope}\,\Delta x)). The Jacobian of the map at the fixed point thus has eigenvalues \lambda \sim -H/(\text{slope}\,\Delta x), about −50 to −600 in our tests, and the under-relaxed iteration is stable only for relax < 2/(1-\lambda), i.e., 0.003–0.04. The bound shrinks with resolution, and routing changes make the map discontinuous. This is a structural property of the method rather than a tuning problem, which is why :steady is the default.

title: Algorithms
text:
10. What was deliberately dropped
Relative to ICESHEET 2.0, the grid Hamilton–Jacobi solver makes the following machinery unnecessary: method-of-characteristics flowline tracing, crossover detection (the motorcycle-graph algorithm), saddle and dome detection with polygon splitting, the GIA and sea-level iteration loop, and the GMT projection and preprocessing pipeline.

title: PlasticIceSheet.jl
text:
PlasticIceSheet.jl reconstructs a perfectly plastic, steady-state ice sheet from three inputs: a grounded-ice mask, a bed elevation z_b and a basal shear stress \tau_b. It returns the ice surface z_s and thickness H, with no time stepping, no climate and no ice dynamics.
It is a simplification and modernization of ICESHEET 2.0 by Evan Gowan and colleagues (source code; Gowan et al., 2016, Geosci. Model Dev.; Gowan et al., 2021, Nat. Commun.). The core physics, one published equation, is retained. The recursive flowline, crossover and saddle machinery of ICESHEET (about 2,600 lines) is replaced by a grid solver of a few hundred lines (Algorithms §10).
The package is meant as a first-guess tool next to a dynamic ice-sheet model (e.g., Yelmo) and an independent GIA and sea-level solver. Typical uses are to initialize a spin-up, to provide a surface for an SMB model, or to serve as a relaxation target.

title: PlasticIceSheet.jl
text:
The idea
Under the perfectly plastic, steady-state assumption the basal shear stress balances the gravitational driving stress, which is set by the geometry:

\tau_b = \tau_d = \rho_i\, g\, H\, |\nabla z_s| .

Rearranging for the surface slope gives the equation we solve,

|\nabla z_s| = \frac{\tau_b}{\rho_i\, g\, (z_s - z_b)} ,

a static Hamilton–Jacobi equation. It is discretized with a monotone upwind scheme and solved by fast sweeping in one pass over the grid, bed relief included. Saddles, domes and coalescing ice caps follow from the upwind (viscosity) solution without flowline tracing or saddle detection (Algorithms §1–6).
Two extensions build on the fixed geometry. A DIVA closure recovers what perfect plasticity discards, a depth-averaged velocity and a first-order surface mass balance (§8). The same flux law then drives the geometry from an SMB instead of a yield stress, by solving steady mass conservation on the prescribed margin (§9).

title: PlasticIceSheet.jl
text:
Quick start
using PlasticIceSheet

nx, ny = 100, 100
dx = dy = 2000.0                                       # grid spacing (m)
z_b  = zeros(nx, ny)                                   # bed elevation (m)
mask = [hypot(i - 50.5, j - 50.5) <= 40 for i in 1:nx, j in 1:ny]
τ_b  = 1.0e5                                           # basal shear stress (Pa)

z_s, H = solve(z_b, τ_b, mask; dx, dy)                 # mode = :surface (default)
A solve on a 300 × 300 grid takes a few milliseconds. The result is differentiable with respect to \tau_b, which enables gradient-based inversion. See Usage for the options, the closures and the examples.
PlasticIceSheet.jl is MIT-licensed. A dependency-free Fortran port for coupling into Fortran models is available as PlasticIceSheet.

title: Inverting basal shear stress
text: The plastic solve turns a margin, a bed and a basal shear stress \tau_b into an ice sheet. \tau_b carries essentially all of the freedom of the reconstruction, so the practical question is the inverse one: which \tau_b makes the reconstruction match the data? This page describes how the inverse problem is posed, the two parameterizations of \tau_b in the examples, and how the tiled parameterization automates the hand-tuned shear-stress domains of ICESHEET (Gowan et al., 2016, 2021). The gradient itself (implicit differentiation of the converged solve) is described in Algorithms §7.

title: Inverting basal shear stress
text:
The inverse problem
We minimize an objective on the reconstruction over \tau_b. For present-day ice the natural target is the observed surface, through surface_misfit:

\min_{\tau_b}\; \big\langle\, (z_s(\tau_b) - z_s^{\text{obs}})^2 \,\big\rangle_{\text{mask}},
\qquad z_s(\tau_b) = z_b + H(\tau_b).

differentiable_thickness gives the gradient by reverse-mode AD, and the examples minimize the misfit with Adam. The grounded mask is the prescribed margin, an input of ICESHEET that is not inverted. The recovered ice extent therefore always equals the mask, and only the geometry inside it is fit.
The number of free parameters in \tau_b should match what the target data can resolve. A dense present-day surface constrains a dense field, while a sparse paleo target (relative sea level) constrains only a few regional values. The two parameterizations below sit at these two ends.

title: Inverting basal shear stress
text:
Two parameterizations
The example examples/invert_taub_greenland.jl implements both and switches between them with the environment variable METHOD:
julia --project=examples examples/invert_taub_greenland.jl                  # METHOD=tiled (default)
METHOD=percell julia --project=examples examples/invert_taub_greenland.jl   # per cell
The objective, the Adam loop and the outputs are shared. Only the map from the optimization parameters to the \tau_b field differs. All results below are for Greenland at 32 km (GRL-32KM, about 2000 ice cells), mode = :surface and margin = :face.

Per cell (METHOD=percell)
A full per-cell \tau_b field is regularized to a length scale REG_KM by a Gaussian-blur reparameterization. We optimize a raw field \varphi and set

\tau_b = \operatorname{clamp}\big(K_x\,\varphi\,K_y\big),

where K_x and K_y are separable 1-D Gaussian smoothers with \sigma = \texttt{REG\_KM}/\Delta x cells. The blur is linear, so it differentiates cleanly under Zygote, and it ensures that \tau_b varies only on scales of at least REG_KM regardless of the data fit. This parameterization has many effective degrees of freedom and fits a dense observed surface closely (about 44 m rmse with REG_KM = 32 km).


Tiled (METHOD=tiled, default)
The tiled parameterization is low-dimensional and transferable to paleo ice sheets. Cells are grouped into tiles defined only from data available for an unknown ice sheet: bed roughness (the windowed standard deviation of z_b, binned into N_ROUGH quantile classes) crossed with a sediment mask (sediment thickness split into soft and hard at SED_THRESH). The ice thickness and ice-derived drainage basins are never used to draw the tiles. Each tile d carries one value \theta_d:

\tau_b(\mathbf x) = \operatorname{clamp}\Big(\textstyle\sum_d \theta_d\, \mathbb 1[\,\mathbf x \in d\,]\Big),

embedded by a one-hot selector matrix, which is linear and thus differentiable under Zygote. The default is N_ROUGH = 4 × 2 sediment classes, i.e., 8 tiles, which reach about 220 m rmse. The observed surface enters only as the calibration target. This is the modern-surface calibration Gowan et al. (2021) used for Greenland and Antarctica, and the place a relative-sea-level objective would take in a paleo reconstruction.

title: Inverting basal shear stress
text:
Relation to ICESHEET
ICESHEET (Gowan et al., 2016) is the same perfectly plastic, equilibrium forward model. In PaleoMIST (Gowan et al., 2021), \tau_b was chosen by three steps. First, the target was relative sea level through a GIA model for the paleo ice sheets, plus geological margins, and the modern surface for Greenland and Antarctica. Second, the shear-stress domains were defined by topographic variability (mountainous or flat) and refined by surficial geology (continuous sediment for low \tau_b, hard or discontinuous cover for high \tau_b). Third, the domain values were tuned by hand until the fit was acceptable.
The tiled method follows this logic but automates both halves: the domains come from bed roughness and sediment, and the domain values come from gradient descent. On Greenland it recovers the premise of Gowan et al.: the soft-sediment tiles settle at about 5–46 kPa and the hard-bed tiles at about 51–99 kPa.

title: Inverting basal shear stress
section: How many tiles? A resolution test
text:
How many tiles? A resolution test
The number of domains, which ICESHEET left to judgement, can be chosen quantitatively. examples/invert_taub_sweep_greenland.jl sweeps the tile count (100 Adam iterations each) and plots the rmse against the number of free parameters. Sediment controls the fit more than roughness does. A single hard/soft split (2 tiles) reduces the rmse from about 320 to 250 m, more than eight roughness-only tiles achieve (about 264 m). The knee lies at about 6 tiles, beyond which further parameters change the rmse by less than 5 m. Even the best tiling (about 210 m) remains well above the per-cell fit (about 44 m). Thus, a substantial part of the surface signal reflects variations of \tau_b that static bed roughness and sediment do not explain, most likely the basal thermal and hydrological state.

title: Inverting basal shear stress
text:
Conditioning: choice of mode
The inversions use mode = :surface, the default. Its scheme is monotone (Algorithms §2), so the residual Jacobian of the adjoint is well conditioned, as for :flat. Including the bed relief, however, improves the fit: with the default 8 tiles :surface reaches about 220 m rmse and :flat about 312 m, at a similar cost (about 4–5 min for 250 iterations). :full is not suitable, since its damped fixed point does not converge on real beds, and its dense adjoint system becomes singular on large grids. For finer grids the cost of the per-cell gradient is dominated by the direct linear solve. See the differentiable_thickness docstring for the iterative-solver option.

title: Inverting basal shear stress
text:
Toward a paleo (RSL) reconstruction
The tiled parameterization links to a paleo reconstruction: keep the bed-derived tiles and replace the observed-surface objective by relative sea level computed with a GIA model. The tiles need no knowledge of the ice sheet, so the same setup transfers to an ice sheet whose geometry is unknown. That is the regime ICESHEET was built for, and the one in which reducing the number of parameters is required rather than optional.
